Given the significant stigma round male suicide and the current study goal to describe men's perspectives of losing a male to suicide, photovoice was adapted as a means to facilitate participant storytelling through both photographs and words (Oliffe & Bottorff, 2007). These visual methods afforded an informal, interactive format to discuss the sensitive and emotionally charged topic of male suicide. The interviews were semistructured, utilizing an interview guide but privileging the participant-produced photographs to drive what was talked about, and ensuring discussion of the issues most important to the men (Oliffe & Bottorff, 2007).

A follow-up in-depth individual interview was scheduled where participants shared and narrated their photographs. Digitally recorded interviews lasting between 60 to 90 minutes were conducted from 2014 to 2016
A total of 20 men [...] who had lost a male to suicide participated in the study.

In contrast, "rationalized suicides" detailed an array of preexisting risk factors including mental illness and/or substance overuse to discuss cause—effect scenarios. Commonalities in unforeseen and rationalized suicides are discussed in the overarching theme, "managing emotions" whereby participants distanced themselves, but also drew meaning from the suicide.

At the same time, it remains unclear how performances of masculinity influence male bereavement in the context of a male suicide. For example, emotional repression, denial, and/or self-medicating through alcohol overuse can be idealized masculine practices deeply relied on by some men, especially in times of crisis, as a means to quell, blunt, or justify emotions (DeVisser, 2009). What this points to is the affective atmosphere and its gendered components, not only in relation to suicide but also with ripple effects post bereavement. That is, the problematic of suicide in men must necessarily be explored beyond the act of suicide itself, to examine the emotional life of men post loss and the ongoing influence of emotional restraint or denial to model alignment with masculine ideals.

First, data coded under the following preliminary categories was retrieved using NVivo: masculine norms, masculine stoicism, and guilt. This data was reviewed, disaggregated, and manually tabled case by case, in conjunction with descriptive fields that included the suicide details, overall emotional tone, the participant's explanation of and response to the death, and exemplary quotes. Then, the author team discussed their interpretations of the data, and based on those conversations and insights, two overall accounts of the suicide were inductively derived: (a) unforeseen suicide and (b) rationalized suicide. Unforeseen suicides were constructed as occurring without warning signs. In contrast, narratives of rationalized suicides drew on an array of preexisting risk factors including mental illness and/or substance overuse to describe contributing issues and cause–effect scenarios. In comparing the interviews allocated to unforeseen and rationalized suicides, commonalities emerged in regard to the participants' management of their suicide-related emotions, and these findings are featured in the overarching theme, managing emotions. The managing emotions theme details men's management strategies including the distancing and meaning making drawn from the suicide.

evidence.section_title: Unforeseen Suicide: "It's All Inside and  Nobody Really Knows"
evidence.quote: Risk: In this context, a selective stoicism or quietness was linked to the deceased with participants pointing to disparities about what the men must really have been feeling and/or experiencing in their life, and leading up to their death. Recovery: I think if all you tell your kids is the good stuff, the great stuff, then that's what they see; they see the good things. Every time they see you as an adult . . . you've kind of got your stuff together. So I think [participant's son], he would see us somewhat struggle, but you don't tell them all of it, maybe you don't remember what it felt like when you were 15.

evidence.section_title: Rationalized Suicide: "I Was a Bit Relieved for  Him, That His Suffering Was Over"
evidence.quote: In contrast to unforeseen cases, other participants rationalized the suicide based on understandings that the deceased had significant contributing circumstances and/or risk factors. Among these cases were men who had been receiving professional mental health care leading up to the suicide. For example, a middle-aged participant whose father shot himself with a rifle explained that his dad had had a long history of severe depression and began taking antidepressant medications 5 days prior to his death. Another participant explained that his friend, who slit his wrists in the bathtub, had been diagnosed with bipolar disorder and was taking medication for a major depressive episode at the time of his death.; I'm not angry with him. In fact, I think I was a bit relieved for him, that his suffering was over . . . I think about him being alive and still struggling . . . I just thought, "He's free, finally he's free" . . . I think that people value themselves and have self-esteem when they can take care of themselves. He was rendered to a point where he couldn't any longer. He became basically indigent. He was reliant on other people and on the province.

evidence.section_title: Managing Emotions: "I Don't Have a Solid  Feeling of That Time"
evidence.quote: ['[page/7/Text/7] Prevailing across the unforeseen and rationalized cases were participants\' actions toward managing their emotions. Often touched upon were men\'s shock, guilt, and/or regret in detailing that they wished they had been able to alter the outcome. However, most participants managed their emotions by detaching themselves from the suicide amid detailing their commitment to avoiding a similar fate.', '[page/8/Text/4] I think women have more of an emotional literacy because it\'s something that\'s modelled and encouraged from a young age . . . it\'s more comfortable for them. I think men experience emotion as deep as women, but have a harder time identifying it for themselves and relating it to other people, and then it becomes an isolating thing . . . I think talking about sadness is saying like, "I don\'t have it figured out, I\'m not in control." I think men . . . really try to keep the lid on it . . . I try to keep the lid on a lot. I think I\'m more than your average emotional male as far as communication, but I still keep a hell of a lot under there.', '[page/8/Text/9] I\'ve got a wife and kids and my wellbeing is not just about myself anymore so I have to be responsible to them and the result of that is I have to suck it up and not be prideful about getting help. And if I have a health or mental issue that I need some help with, get it taken care of because I need to be there not only for myself but for other people.', '[page/8/Text/12] Participants\' commitment to being healthy and open to receiving help when necessary was also positioned as protective against suicide.']

For example, within the context of unforeseen suicides, participants grappled with accepting the deceased men's agency to self-manage; even though such strategies had failed, there was recognition that men who solicited "outside" help were at risk of being seen as weak. In their tacit fluency with masculine ideals, positioning self-reliance as strength-based and health help-seeking as synonymous with weakness, it was clear that participants understood some of the strategies used and challenges faced by the deceased.There was, however, little interrogation about how these same masculine ideals may have limited men, preventing them from reaching out to more fully connect with one another. Related to this were participants' acceptance of and alignments to emotional privacy or stoicism versus expressivity and relating wholly with other men. Reminders abound here regarding the influence of as well as the tensions in and around dominant ideals of masculinity.However, in contrast to Cook (1988) and Martin and Doka (2000, 2011) who argued against construing such approaches as deficits or maladaptive male coping strategies, we suggest that there are some benefits to loosening the constraints of stoicism among men bereaved by suicide. In essence, without assuming emotional expressivity (Martin & Doka, 2000, 2011) as the gold standard for healthy grieving, facilitating men's talk about suicide can norm such discussions, and provide important permissions for men to speak up and about ordinarily taboo issues in destigmatizing ways.Related to this point, the men's feedback about participating in the current photovoice study was overwhelmingly positive, with many men asserting the therapeutic value of talking about their experiences of losing a male to suicide. Drawing from this methodological lesson, it is important for everyone, including health care professionals, researchers, family, and friends, to recognize that while men bereaved by male suicide may feel compelled to restrain their emotions (for themselves and others), it is critical that we all use our influence to make available, and affirm, diverse avenues for men to grieve.
